title: Concerto for Violin and Cello in A minor, “Double Concerto”
hook: Brahms’s last orchestral work, written to make peace with an old friend.

painting.title: Lake Thun with Symmetrical Reflection
painting.pairingNote: Lake Thun, where Brahms spent the summer of 1887 writing the concerto, with the mountains and their mirror image answering each other like the violin and the cello.

facts: Brahms wrote the concerto in the summer of 1887 at Lake Thun in Switzerland. It was his last work for orchestra. The first performance was in Cologne on 18 October 1887, with the violinist Joseph Joachim, the cellist Robert Hausmann and Brahms conducting.

Brahms and Joachim had been friends for more than thirty years, but they fell out when Joachim divorced his wife, Amalie, and Brahms took her side. The concerto was in part a peace offering. Brahms gave Joachim the manuscript inscribed “To him for whom it was written”.

Two soloists share the stage, and Brahms makes them sound like partners. They pass phrases back and forth, play in octaves, and sometimes run their scales together so that they sound like one huge string instrument.
The early reception was cool; even Clara Schumann found it “not brilliant for the instruments”. Today it is a favourite of violin and cello pairs.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a dramatic dialogue that starts with two cadenzas (I), a warm song in octaves (II), a Hungarian-flavoured rondo that ends in A major (III).

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: The orchestra barely starts before it stops, and the cello speaks alone in a long [[cadenza|cadenza]]; then the violin joins it. Only after this double introduction does the orchestra set out the themes properly. The movement is a [[sonata-form|sonata form]] with a [[double-exposition|double exposition]], and the two soloists spend it in close, sometimes stormy, conversation.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a strong, falling theme with a long-short rhythm, first in the full orchestra and then in the cello.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a tender, sighing melody first hinted at by the violin in its cadenza.

mainIdeas.name: The syncopated repeated notes
mainIdeas.description: an urgent, off-beat figure that drives the transitions.

notice: The concerto opens like an argument: the orchestra starts, then falls silent while first the cello and then the violin have their say alone.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: David Oistrakh and Mstislav Rostropovich recorded the concerto with George Szell and the Cleveland Orchestra in Severance Hall in May 1969. The orchestra says the LP, released in 1970, won a Grammy award.

movements.heading: Andante
movements.summary: A short, warm song. After a horn call, violin and cello play the melody together, an octave apart, as if they were one voice. A middle section for the woodwinds is calm and hymn-like; the violin then wanders in a gentle daydream before the song returns.

mainIdeas.name: The horn call
mainIdeas.description: two rising notes, answered by the woodwinds.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a broad, arching melody for violin and cello in octaves.

mainIdeas.name: The middle section
mainIdeas.description: a quiet, hymn-like tune for flutes, clarinets and bassoons.

stops.hear: A rising horn call, answered by the woodwinds
Violin and cello together, an octave apart, sing a broad, arching melody
The soloists fall silent; flutes, clarinets and bassoons play a calm, hymn-like tune

stops.hear: The violin enters with a slow, dreamy line in triplets
stops.happening: A daydream over the woodwind tune

stops.hear: The two soloists alone, in a short, quiet passage
The arching melody again, over plucked strings

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The horn call in reverse, a soft D major chord

notice: In the main theme, listen for the violin and cello playing the same melody an octave apart. It is one tune, but with the depth of two instruments.

movements.heading: Vivace non troppo
movements.summary: A [[rondo|rondo]] with a Hungarian flavour. The cello starts the jaunty main theme, the violin repeats it, and the orchestra joins in with full force. Between its returns come a noble, stately theme and a dramatic central section. The minor turns to A major at the end.

mainIdeas.name: The rondo theme
mainIdeas.description: a jaunty, slightly gypsy-style tune with a long-short-short rhythm.

mainIdeas.name: The noble theme
mainIdeas.description: broad and stately, first played by the cello in [[double-stop|double stop]]s.

stops.hear: The cello alone, over quiet low strings, plays a jaunty, dancing tune
stops.happening: The rondo theme, in A minor

stops.hear: The violin repeats the tune, higher
The whole orchestra bursts in with the tune
The cello plays a broad, stately melody in two-note chords; then the violin
The jaunty tune returns in the cello
An abrupt, powerful turn to the minor; the soloists play together with force
A gentle melody in the woodwinds, with rippling arpeggios from the soloists
stops.happening: A calm theme inside the central episode

stops.hear: The cello begins the jaunty tune once more
The stately melody again, now in A major, with both soloists

notice: Compare the opening tune with its last appearance in the woodwinds near the end. The same notes, but the dance has become a dream, and the minor has become major.

threads.title: Two voices, one friendship
threads.body: Violin and cello argue, answer and finally join in octaves. Brahms wrote it for Joachim, the friend he had lost, and for the cellist of Joachim’s quartet.

threads.title: A–E–F
threads.body: The concerto uses the notes A, E and F, a reordering of F–A–E, Joachim’s old motto “free but lonely”. In 1853 Brahms had used those notes in a sonata for Joachim written together with Robert Schumann and Albert Dietrich.

threads.title: The last orchestral work
threads.body: After this Brahms wrote no more symphonies or concertos. He turned to chamber music, piano pieces and songs.
